label: Psychology
title: Why We Defend Our Mistakes – Cognitive Dissonance and the Stories We Tell Ourselves
description: What happens when a group's prophecy fails – and they believe even more strongly afterwards? In this calm video essay we look at Leon Festinger's theory of cognitive dissonance, the undercover study of a doomsday group in 1954, the famous one-dollar experiment, Aesop's fox and the sour grapes, and Benjamin Franklin's clever trick with a borrowed book. Plus a simple way to notice self-justification before it takes over.

sections.text:
On the evening of December 20, 1954, a small group of people sat together in a house near Chicago and waited.

They had given up jobs, money and friendships for what they believed was coming. Before dawn, a great flood would destroy much of the world. But they would be saved. At midnight, a flying saucer would arrive and take them away.

Midnight came. Nothing happened. Then one o'clock. Then two.

What would you expect people to do when a prophecy fails so completely? Most of us would say: they admit they were wrong.

But among the people sitting quietly in that room were researchers in disguise. And what they saw would change how we understand the human mind.

sections.heading: When Prophecy Fails
sections.text:
The psychologists were Leon Festinger, Henry Riecken and Stanley Schachter. They had read about the group in a newspaper and joined it undercover, together with a few assistants, to see what would happen after the predicted day.

The group's leader, a woman from the Chicago area whom the researchers called Marian Keech, said she received messages from beings on another planet. Before the deadline, the group had mostly avoided publicity.

Then came the long night. Hours after midnight, with the group in visible distress, the leader received a new message. Because of the faith of this small group, it said, the world had been spared.

And now something remarkable happened. The group, which had avoided the press, began calling newspapers. They wanted to spread the message. The failure had not weakened the belief of the most committed members. For them, it seemed to make it stronger.

The researchers published their account in 1956 in a book called When Prophecy Fails. It has its critics. The researchers were not neutral observers, and their presence may have influenced the group they were studying. But the pattern they described has been found again and again since.

sections.heading: A Theory of Discomfort
sections.text:
A year later, in 1957, Festinger gave the pattern a name. He called it cognitive dissonance.

The idea is simple. When we hold two thoughts that do not fit together, we feel an unpleasant tension. I am a sensible person. I just gave up everything for a prophecy that failed. Both cannot comfortably be true at the same time.

And so the mind looks for a way out. The easiest way is often not to change our behavior, which has already happened, but to change the story we tell about it. We were not wrong. Our faith saved the world.

The more we have invested, the stronger the pull. A small mistake is easy to admit. A mistake that cost us years, money or our reputation can feel almost impossible to face.

sections.heading: The One-Dollar Experiment
sections.text:
Two years later, Festinger and his student James Carlsmith tested the idea in a laboratory at Stanford.

They gave students an hour of deliberately boring tasks. Putting spools on a tray and taking them off again. Turning pegs on a board, a quarter turn at a time.

Afterwards, each student was asked to tell the next participant that the tasks had been interesting and enjoyable. Some were paid one dollar for this small lie. Others were paid twenty dollars, a lot of money at the time.

Later, all of them were asked how much they had actually enjoyed the tasks. You might expect the twenty-dollar group to be the most positive. It was the opposite. The students who were paid only one dollar rated the boring tasks as more enjoyable.

Festinger's explanation was this. Twenty dollars is a good reason to tell a small lie. One dollar is not. So the students with one dollar had a dissonance to resolve, and many of them did it quietly, by deciding that the task had not been so bad after all.

sections.heading: Sour Grapes

quote.lead: None of this is entirely new. One of Aesop's oldest fables describes the same move in a few lines.
quote.text: A hungry fox saw bunches of grapes hanging from a vine and wanted to get them, but could not. As she went away, she said to herself: They are unripe.
quote.author: Aesop, The Fox and the Grapes

sections.text:
The fable ends with a short lesson. In the same way, some people who cannot reach something through their own weakness blame the circumstances.

The fox does not change the grapes. She changes what she believes about them. And it works. She can walk away without feeling like a failure.

Psychologists later found the same thing in everyday choices. In a study from 1956, the psychologist Jack Brehm asked participants to rate household products, things like a toaster or a coffee maker,, and then let them choose one of two to take home. Afterwards, they rated the product they had chosen higher than before, and the one they had left behind lower. Once a decision is made, we quietly polish the option we picked and find small flaws in the one we rejected.

This is not always bad. It helps us live with our choices instead of endlessly doubting them. The problem begins when the same mechanism keeps us from learning.

sections.heading: Franklin's Borrowed Book

quote.lead: Dissonance can also work in surprising directions. Benjamin Franklin described how he won over a hostile rival in the Pennsylvania legislature. He did not flatter him. He asked to borrow a rare book from his library.
quote.text: He that has once done you a kindness will be more ready to do you another, than he whom you yourself have obliged.
quote.author: Benjamin Franklin, Autobiography

sections.text:
Franklin called it an old maxim. The rival lent him the book, Franklin returned it with a warm note of thanks, and from then on the man treated him with a new kindness. According to Franklin, they remained friends until the rival's death.

Seen through Festinger's theory, it makes sense. I did a favor for this man. Why would I do that for someone I dislike? Perhaps he is not so bad after all.

The same mind that defends our mistakes can also soften our hostility. Our actions shape our beliefs, not only the other way around.

sections.heading: Noticing the Story
sections.text:
So how do we notice dissonance before it quietly rewrites our story? Here are three small habits.

First, watch for the sudden certainty. When you catch yourself defending something with unusual energy, especially something that cost you a lot, pause. Then ask: Am I defending the idea, or my decision to believe it?

Second, separate your choices from your identity. I made a bad decision is a much easier sentence than I am a bad decision maker. The first can be corrected. The second has to be defended.

Third, practice saying three short words: I was wrong. The psychologists Carol Tavris and Elliot Aronson, who wrote a whole book on self-justification, argue that admitting a mistake is not a sign of weakness. It is what keeps a mind open to learning. Each time we justify a small error, the next one becomes a little easier to justify.

The people in that room in 1954 were not foolish. They were human, and they had invested everything. Most of us do the same thing on a smaller scale, every day.

The goal is not to never feel dissonance. It is to notice the moment when we start polishing the grapes, and to look at them once more, honestly.

short.title: What happened when a doomsday prophecy failed
short.text:
In December 1954, a small group near Chicago waited for a flying saucer to save them from the end of the world. Midnight came. Nothing happened.

Among them were psychologists in disguise. They expected the group to admit they were wrong.

Instead, the most committed members believed even more strongly, and began calling newspapers to spread the message.

Leon Festinger called it cognitive dissonance. When reality clashes with what we have invested in, we often do not change our minds. We change the story.

The next time you defend something with unusual energy, ask yourself: am I defending the idea, or my decision?
